origin_region: Nantou · Mingjian and lower Chiayi slopes
processing: Lightly oxidised (roughly 15–20%), ball-rolled and dried without roasting; occasionally made as a twisted Bao Zhong-style tea or fully oxidised as a black.
harvest_season: Spring and winter at best; lowland gardens pick it several times a year and sell summer lots cheaply.
appearance_dry: Tight, dark-green balls slightly larger than Qing Xin, with a bright, high floral smell on the dry leaf.
appearance_liquor: Pale yellow with a green tinge, bright and clear.
appearance_wet: Large, broad, darker-green leaves with a slightly glossy surface and a faint red rim.
taste_profile: An intense white-flower perfume between gardenia and ginger lily over a light, bright body with a sweet finish and little of Jin Xuan's creaminess.

brewing.notes: Water just off the boil and short steeps; five infusions is about its range. Lovely cold-brewed, where the florals stay clean.

vintage_note: Sold by cultivar name and season, spring and winter of the current year at best and year-round from the lowlands, usually in vacuum packs at modest prices. Because it is uncommon it is more often an honest single-cultivar product than a disguise for something else; drink it within a year.
description:
Cui Yu, 'jade green', is Taiwan Tea Experiment Station cultivar number 13, released in 1981 in the same batch as Jin Xuan and, by the usual telling, named after breeder Wu Zhenduo's mother where Jin Xuan honoured his grandmother. It never caught on to the same degree, so it is the one of the pair you need to look for, mostly in the Mingjian lowlands of Nantou and on the lower Alishan slopes.

The bush is a cross of the local Ying Zhi Hong Xin cultivar and a research-station line, vigorous and high-yielding, with larger, darker leaves than Qing Xin. It is almost always made as a lightly oxidised, ball-rolled oolong with no roast, occasionally as a twisted Bao Zhong-style tea, and the point of it is aroma: the station described it as smelling of wild ginger lily and betel-palm flower, and the cup really is that floral.

Expect an intense white-flower perfume, somewhere between gardenia and ginger lily, over a light, bright body with a sweet finish and little of the creaminess that Jin Xuan has. It is a fragrant, easy tea rather than a deep one. Brew with water just off the boil and short steeps; five infusions is about its range, and it is lovely cold-brewed.

It is sold by cultivar name and season, spring and winter at best, year-round from the lowlands, usually in vacuum packs and at modest prices; because it is uncommon, it is more often an honest single-cultivar product than a disguise for something else. Drink it within a year.

Taste it side by side with Jin Xuan to understand what the breeders were after: the same year, the same programme, one bush for texture and one for perfume.
sources_note: Parentage (Ying Zhi Hong Xin x Tainong 80 line) and the 'named after Wu's mother' story are from memory; the ginger-lily / betel-flower aroma description follows TRES cultivar notes.
